analysis.one_liner: Caps House campaign spending at $600,000 with public matching funds and bans bundling and leadership PAC money.
analysis.headline: The House campaign finance reform bill never got a hearing or vote in the House Administration Committee, dying with no cosponsors during the 103rd Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have let House candidates voluntarily accept a $600,000 spending cap in exchange for public matching funds from a 'Make Democracy Work' fund, tightened limits on PAC and large-donor money, banned bundling and leadership PACs, and toughened disclosure and ad rules. It was a voluntary system — candidates who stayed out kept spending freely. It never received a hearing or a vote in the House Administration Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Non-wealthy candidates could run competitive House races without courting big donors, and voters would get fuller disclosure of where campaign money came from.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a voluntary $600,000 spending and contribution limit for House candidates in exchange for public matching funds of up to $200,000, letting candidates run without relying on large donors.
Caps PAC and large-donor contributions at $200,000 per election cycle, curbs 'bundling' of contributions by intermediaries, and bans incumbent 'leadership' PACs.
Closes loopholes including foreign-national influence, state/local party money, and false fundraising solicitation.
Tightens disclosure by lowering the donor identification threshold to $50 and requiring FEC to maintain computerized indices of contributions of $50 or more.

analysis.who_pays: The U.S. Treasury pays for matching funds, subject to budget-neutrality offsets like limits on lobbying tax deductibility and FEC registration fees.

drawbacks.text: The system is voluntary; candidates who decline the cap — including self-funded millionaires and outside-spending groups — face no limits, and matching funds are triggered only when independent spending crosses low thresholds.
Public matching funds draw only from revenue offsets such as limiting lobbying tax deductibility and FEC fees, so adequacy of the fund depends on those uncertain revenue measures.
FEC eligibility, audit, and enforcement of the spending cap add administrative complexity and compliance costs for campaigns.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would mainly have benefited candidates without personal wealth and voters wanting cleaner campaigns, at a modest public cost that the bill itself insists be offset with revenue measures. Its biggest design weakness is the voluntary structure, which leaves unlimited spending untouched for anyone who opts out — a real problem outside groups and wealthy opponents could exploit. Still, it set up a plausible public financing model for House races that never got a hearing, let alone a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Committee on House Administration the day it was introduced, was never marked up or reported out, and received no hearing or floor vote before the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Romano Mazzoli (D-KY) introduced H.R. 275 on January 5, 1993, and it was referred to the House Committee on House Administration.
Mazzoli gave introductory remarks in support of the bill on the House floor in March and again in November 1993, but no further legislative action followed.
The bill never received a committee markup, a vote, or consideration by the full House during the 103rd Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent officeholders and well-funded campaigns — including those benefiting from large-donor and leadership PAC money — were better off because the bill died, since the spending caps, PAC limits, and ban on leadership PACs never took effect. Ordinary voters lost a chance at public financing and tighter campaign finance rules.

for.name: Rep. Romano Mazzoli
for.role: House Representative from Kentucky's 3rd district, sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced H.R. 275 on January 5, 1993, and gave two sets of introductory floor remarks (March and November 1993) supporting the bill.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over campaign finance and election law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral January 5, 1993, and never marked it up, held a hearing, or reported it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no party breakdown exists; it attracted no cosponsors from either party, and the committee of jurisdiction did not act on it.

industries.industry: Political action committees and large-donor interests
industries.note: Caps total PAC and large-donor contributions at $200,000 per cycle and bans bundling, sharply reducing a channel for concentrated money to influence House races.

industries.industry: Incumbent officeholders with large campaign accounts
industries.note: Excess funds above $600,000 must be set aside and not used for the House election, limiting incumbents' fundraising edge.
Requires lowest-unit ad rates and prohibits preempting candidate ads, reducing ad revenue in election windows, while spending limits cap total ad buys.
Matching funds are publicly financed, though the bill requires cost offsets via measures like limiting lobbying tax deductibility.
